question: What attorney fees and costs are involved in collection cases?
answer: Contingency fees can be advantageous when the likelihood of success is uncertain and if you don't want to pay money on a retainer. The usual contingency fee to collect the debt is between 20 and 30%, depending on the amount of the debt. With the contingency fee you would pay nothing if the debt is not collected.

However, if you have a reasonable expectation of recovering the amount owed, a reasonable hourly attorney fee may save on your bottom line. Of importance to note for creditors: if you have language in your contract to collect attorney's fees upon default, a court will most likely grant reasonable attorney fees. Courts will even grant attorney fees in the amount of the contingency fee you are charged by your attorney. In any event, it is important to have an experienced debt collection attorney to help you collect your debts.

question: What’s the difference between wills and a trust?
answer: A will is a simple legal document that provides instructions on how to distribute property to beneficiaries after death. A will is only viable upon death and needs to be probated upon death. Probate is the process where the executor goes to a branch of the court to be sworn in as executor. The court will provide you with what rules you must follow to administer the will.

A trust is a legal contract that allows assets to be transferred to a trustee for management. In the case of a revocable trust, you (or, if married, you and your spouse) are the person who can be the trustee and run the trust. If you are married and you or your spouse become incapacitated or pass away, the other spouse remains as trustee and runs the trust. When both spouses pass away or become incapacitated, a successor trustee who you choose will automatically by contract step in and run the trust without probate or guardianship proceedings. You may amend these trusts at any time. Revocable trusts are designed to avoid probate and make assets more easily distributable and immediately liquid without any court intervention.

Irrevocable trusts are designed to protect assets from creditors, including Medicaid. The main difference between revocable trusts and irrevocable trusts is that the person or spouses who set up the trust cannot be the trustees. So, you lose control of the assets you put in the trust. Irrevocable trusts cannot be changed. However, there are special protections for you as the person who sets up the trust in the event the law changes or the intent of the trust changes.
